findings.title: Unhandled ValueError from invalid hex chunk length in chunked body reader
findings.description: In `_read_chunked_body`, the chunk length is parsed with `int(chunk_len_str.strip(), 16)` at line 663. If a client sends a non-hexadecimal value (e.g., 'xyz\r\n'), this raises a bare `ValueError` that is not caught anywhere in `_read_chunked_body` or `_read_message`. The `except httputil.HTTPInputError` block in `_read_message` (line 288) does not catch `ValueError`, so the exception propagates to `_server_request_loop` where it hits the generic `except Exception` handler (line 825), logs an uncaught exception, and closes the connection without sending a 400 response. Malformed chunk sizes should raise `httputil.HTTPInputError` instead.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the `int(chunk_len_str.strip(), 16)` call in a try/except ValueError and raise `httputil.HTTPInputError('Invalid chunk size')` instead, so it is handled gracefully with a 400 response.

findings.title: assert used to validate protocol data (chunk trailing CRLF)
findings.description: At line 687, `assert crlf == b'\r\n'` is used to verify that each chunk in a chunked-encoded body is followed by CRLF. If Python is run with the `-O` (optimize) flag, assertions are stripped and this check is silently skipped, allowing malformed chunked bodies to be accepted without error. Even without `-O`, this raises `AssertionError` rather than `httputil.HTTPInputError`, which is not caught by the `except httputil.HTTPInputError` handler and will propagate as an unhandled exception, causing the server to log an error and close the connection ungracefully instead of returning a 400.
findings.suggestion: Replace the assert with an explicit check: `if crlf != b'\r\n': raise httputil.HTTPInputError('improperly terminated chunk')`

findings.title: Potential NameError: resp_start_line used in body reading even on server side
findings.description: At line 252-254, `_read_body` is called with `resp_start_line.code if self.is_client else 0`. However, `resp_start_line` is only assigned at line 201 when `self.is_client` is True (inside the `if self.is_client:` block at line 199). On the server side (`self.is_client == False`), `resp_start_line` is never assigned, so if Python evaluates the ternary expression at all, it references an unbound name. In practice the `else` branch of the ternary avoids accessing `resp_start_line` when not `is_client`, but this is fragile and could cause a `NameError`/`UnboundLocalError` if the code is ever refactored.
findings.suggestion: Use a local variable initialized to None at the top of the function or restructure to avoid the conditional reference to a potentially unbound variable. E.g., `code = resp_start_line.code if self.is_client else 0` with `resp_start_line` safely defaulted.

findings.title: HTTP response header injection via newline check on encoded bytes only
findings.description:
At lines 446-449, header lines are encoded to bytes (latin1) and then checked for `b'
'`. However, the check only catches literal newline bytes in the encoded output. If a header name or value contains a carriage return `` without a following newline (or other header-injection sequences that survive latin1 encoding), those are not caught. Furthermore, the check applies to the fully formatted `name: value` string but not to the raw header names and values individually before concatenation, meaning a crafted header name containing `
` followed by an injected header might slip through if the newline appears after a colon in the name. While the `
` check offers some protection, it is incomplete: ``-only injections are not blocked.
findings.suggestion: Validate both header names and values individually for `\r` and `\n` characters before encoding. Use `if b'\r' in line or b'\n' in line: raise ValueError(...)` or validate prior to formatting.

findings.title: Negative Content-Length values not rejected
findings.description: At line 621, `content_length > self._max_body_size` is checked but there is no check for `content_length < 0`. A request with `Content-Length: -1` would pass the upper-bound check and be passed to `_read_fixed_body` with a negative `content_length`. The `while content_length > 0` loop in `_read_fixed_body` (line 647) would immediately exit (since -1 > 0 is False), so no body is read. This could allow a request to bypass body processing or desynchronize the connection state.
findings.suggestion: Add a check: `if content_length < 0: raise httputil.HTTPInputError('Negative Content-Length')` after parsing the integer value.

findings.title: Regex used in read_until_regex for header terminator may be slow on pathological input
findings.description: The regex `b'\r?\n\r?\n'` passed to `read_until_regex` at line 183-184 is simple and unlikely to cause catastrophic backtracking. However, `read_until_regex` may buffer up to `max_header_size` bytes while scanning, and a client that sends data that nearly matches the pattern but doesn't terminate could cause the server to buffer the full `max_header_size` bytes before raising an error. This is mitigated by the `max_bytes` parameter and the `header_timeout`, but is worth noting.
findings.suggestion: This is largely mitigated by existing defenses (max_bytes, header_timeout). No urgent change required, but ensure header_timeout is always configured in production.

findings.title: Gzip decompression bomb: no limit on decompressed data size
findings.description: In `_GzipMessageDelegate.data_received` (lines 723-738), compressed data is decompressed in a loop with no limit on the total size of decompressed output. A malicious client can send a small gzip-compressed payload that expands to an arbitrarily large amount of data (a 'zip bomb'). While `_max_body_size` limits the compressed input, there is no corresponding limit on the decompressed output size, allowing memory exhaustion attacks.
findings.suggestion: Track the total decompressed bytes and raise an error if they exceed `_max_body_size` or a configurable decompressed size limit.

findings.title: Mutable default argument `set()` shared across all callers
findings.description: The parameter `exclude` in `serialize_response` (line 78) uses `set()` as its default value. In Python, mutable default arguments are evaluated once at function definition time and shared across all invocations that rely on the default. If any caller or internal code mutates this set, it will corrupt the default for all subsequent calls that do not pass an explicit value. The same pattern recurs at lines 131, 255, 399, 456, 600, 651, 702, 753, 804, 855, 906, and 957.
findings.suggestion: Use `None` as the default and assign an empty set/dict inside the function body: `exclude: Union[SetIntStr, DictIntStrAny] = None` then `exclude = exclude or set()`.

findings.title: Mutable default argument `set()` for `response_model_exclude` in `get_request_handler`
findings.description: The parameter `response_model_exclude` in `get_request_handler` uses a bare `set()` as its default. This singleton set object is shared across all calls that omit this argument. Mutation of the set by any downstream code will silently affect all subsequent route handler invocations.
findings.suggestion: Replace `set()` default with `None` and initialize inside the function body.

findings.title: Non-deterministic `unique_id` generation when `methods` is a `Set`
findings.description: At line 271, `list(methods)[0]` is used to pick the first method for generating `unique_id`. When `methods` is a `Set[str]` (which is explicitly allowed by the type annotation `Optional[Union[Set[str], List[str]]]`), iteration order is implementation-defined and non-deterministic across Python runs (especially with hash randomization). This means the `unique_id` and consequently `operation_id` and response field names may differ across server restarts, breaking client tooling that caches OpenAPI operation IDs.
findings.suggestion: Sort or normalize the methods collection before indexing: `method=sorted(methods)[0]` or convert to a sorted list early in `__init__`.

findings.title: Use of `assert` for runtime invariant enforcement bypassed with `-O` flag
findings.description: Multiple `assert` statements (lines 116, 136, 208, 275, 310, 313, 332, 522) are used to enforce runtime invariants and validate developer-supplied configurations. When Python is run with the `-O` (optimize) flag, all `assert` statements are stripped. This means critical checks — such as verifying that `dependant.call` is not None, that status codes with no body are not paired with response models, and that path prefixes are valid — are silently skipped, potentially causing obscure runtime failures or security bypasses downstream.
findings.suggestion: Replace `assert` with explicit `if` checks that raise appropriate exceptions (e.g., `ValueError`, `TypeError`, or `HTTPException`) for all runtime invariant enforcement.

findings.title: Empty-prefix validation only checks routes with a `path` attribute of `None` or empty string inconsistently
findings.description: At lines 527-533, when `prefix` is empty, the code uses `getattr(r, 'path')` (without a default), which will raise `AttributeError` if a route object lacks a `path` attribute. Furthermore, the condition `if path is not None and not path` checks for an empty string only when path is not None — but `getattr(r, 'path')` without a default will throw `AttributeError` for routes that genuinely lack this attribute (e.g., `Mount` objects or custom route types). The guard should use `getattr(r, 'path', None)` to be safe.
findings.suggestion: Use `getattr(r, 'path', None)` to avoid `AttributeError` on route types that may not have a `path` attribute.

findings.title: Mutable default argument `set()` for `response_model_exclude` in `APIRoute.__init__`
findings.description: The `response_model_exclude` parameter of `APIRoute.__init__` uses a mutable `set()` as its default argument. This is shared across all instantiations that omit the argument, and any mutation of this object will corrupt defaults for all future instantiations.
findings.suggestion: Use `None` as the default and assign `set()` inside the constructor body if the value is `None`.

findings.title: Raw JSON body parsed without size or content-type validation
findings.description: At line 184, `await request.json()` is called unconditionally on any non-empty body whenever a body field is expected. There is no validation of Content-Type header before attempting JSON parsing. A client sending a non-JSON Content-Type (e.g., `application/xml`) with a body will still trigger JSON parsing. While `json.JSONDecodeError` is caught, other exceptions from the JSON parsing stage (e.g., memory errors from a huge payload) fall through to the generic `except Exception` handler at line 187 which returns a generic 400, potentially masking real issues. More critically, there is no body size limit enforced here, leaving the endpoint vulnerable to large-body denial-of-service if Starlette's default limits are not configured.
findings.suggestion: Validate the Content-Type header before attempting JSON parsing. Consider enforcing body size limits at the middleware level or within the handler. Also ensure the `json.JSONDecodeError` catch at line 185 uses `raise ... from e` for proper exception chaining.

findings.title: JSONDecodeError exception raised without chaining (missing 'from e')
findings.description: At line 186, a `RequestValidationError` is raised inside the `except json.JSONDecodeError as e` handler without using `raise ... from e`. This discards the original exception's traceback context, making debugging harder and potentially suppressing useful diagnostic information. The static analysis tool (B904) flagged this pattern. When Python raises an exception inside an `except` block without `from`, it does set `__context__` implicitly, but the intent is unclear and the traceback display may be confusing.
findings.suggestion: Change line 186 to: `raise RequestValidationError([ErrorWrapper(e, ("body", e.pos))], body=e.doc) from e`

findings.title: Non-deterministic operation ID generation when multiple HTTP methods are specified
findings.description: At line 316, `list(methods)[0]` is used to pick the first HTTP method for generating the `unique_id`. However, `methods` at this point has already been converted to a `set` at line 314 (`self.methods = set([method.upper() for method in methods])`). Sets in Python do not preserve insertion order, so when multiple methods are provided (e.g., `["GET", "POST"]`), the first element of `list(self.methods)` (note: `methods` here still refers to the original parameter, not the set, but the original `methods` list is used) — actually looking more carefully, on line 316 `list(methods)[0]` refers to the `methods` parameter (not `self.methods`), so if `methods` was originally a list, the order is preserved. However, if `methods` was passed as a `Set[str]`, then iteration order is undefined. This creates a non-deterministic `unique_id` when `methods` is passed as a set with multiple values, which can result in different OpenAPI operation IDs across restarts, breaking client tooling.
findings.suggestion: Explicitly sort the methods before picking the first one: `method=sorted(methods)[0]` or `method=list(sorted(self.methods))[0]`. This ensures a stable, deterministic operation ID regardless of how methods are passed.

findings.title: status_code converted from IntEnum but type annotation still accepts non-int enum values
findings.description: At lines 306-307, `status_code` is converted from `enum.IntEnum` to `int`. However, the parameter type annotation is `int` (line 281), and a plain `enum.Enum` (non-int) could be passed. If a non-IntEnum `enum.Enum` with an integer value is passed, the `isinstance(status_code, enum.IntEnum)` check would be False and the raw Enum object would be stored as `self.status_code`, potentially causing unexpected behavior when compared against `STATUS_CODES_WITH_NO_BODY` or used in response generation.
findings.suggestion: Broaden the check to `isinstance(status_code, enum.Enum)` and use `status_code = status_code.value` to handle all enum types, or add input validation to reject non-int-compatible enum values.

findings.title: Background tasks lost when endpoint returns a Response with existing background tasks
findings.description: At lines 205-208, when `raw_response` is an instance of `Response`, the handler only assigns `background_tasks` if `raw_response.background is None`. findings.title: Dead code: `value is None` check after `isinstance(value, datetime)` is always False
findings.description: In `convert_value`, the `elif isinstance(value, datetime)` branch at line 325 is entered only when `value` is a `datetime` instance. However, the very first nested check inside this branch is `if value is None` (line 326), which can never be True since `isinstance(None, datetime)` is always `False`. The intended guard — handling a `None` value for DateField/TimeField output — is therefore unreachable dead code. The real consequence is that if `value` is `None` and `self.output_field` is a `DateField` or `TimeField` (not `DateTimeField`), the code falls through the `elif isinstance(value, datetime)` branch without entering it (correct), but the comment/intent shows the developer intended to short-circuit for `None`. More critically, the conditions at lines 328–331 that call `value.date()` or `value.time()` are only reached when `value` is a `datetime`, so those are safe; but the ordering of conditions means the `None` guard for non-DateTimeField output types is illogical and misleading. If a database returns `None` for a DateField or TimeField output, `convert_value` silently returns `None` which is acceptable, but if a database returns a `datetime` for a DateField output, `value.date()` is called correctly. The real bug is the inverted logic: `if value is None: pass` followed by the real processing, which is a no-op guard that obscures intent and could be a ported logic error where the `None` check should have come before the `isinstance` check.

findings.title: LIKE-pattern injection via unsanitized value in filter functions
findings.description: All seven MySQL filter functions (mysql_contains, mysql_starts_with, mysql_ends_with, mysql_insensitive_exact, mysql_insensitive_contains, mysql_insensitive_starts_with, mysql_insensitive_ends_with) interpolate the `value` parameter directly into LIKE-pattern strings using f-strings (e.g., `f"%{value}%"`). MySQL LIKE patterns treat `%` and `_` as wildcards. If a caller passes a value containing `%` or `_`, the resulting LIKE clause will match more rows than intended. For example, a value of `%` in mysql_contains produces `LIKE "%%%"`, which matches every row. This allows users to craft filter inputs that bypass intended filtering constraints and extract more data than authorized, constituting a LIKE wildcard injection vulnerability. The `value` should be escaped so that literal `%` and `_` characters in the search term are treated as literals (e.g., via `value.replace('%', '\\%').replace('_', '\\_')`).
findings.suggestion: Escape LIKE metacharacters (`%` and `_`) in `value` before interpolation. For example: `escaped = value.replace('\\', '\\\\').replace('%', '\\%').replace('_', '\\_')` and then use `escaped` in the f-string pattern. Additionally ensure the ESCAPE clause is passed to the LIKE expression if PyPika supports it.

findings.title: Potential NoneType AttributeError when pk_field_object is None
findings.description: In `_process_insert_result`, `pk_field_object` is assigned from `self.model._meta.pk` (line 63). If the model has no primary key defined, `self.model._meta.pk` may return `None`. The subsequent `isinstance` check on line 65 will safely return `False` for `None`, so that specific line is safe. However, accessing `.generated` on a `None` object at line 66 would only be reached if `isinstance` returned `True`, which it would not for `None`. The real risk is that `pk_field_object` being `None` is silently swallowed with no indication that the insert result was not processed, which could lead to `instance.pk` remaining unset after a successful insert, causing downstream `AttributeError` or incorrect behavior when the caller relies on `instance.pk` being populated.
findings.suggestion: Add an explicit guard: `if pk_field_object is None: return` or log a warning when the model has no auto-generated integer primary key, so callers are informed that `instance.pk` will not be set.

findings.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via unescaped directory listing output
findings.description: The `_directory_as_html` method constructs an HTML directory listing by directly interpolating file names and paths into HTML without any escaping. On lines 679, 686-687, 691-693, and 696-698, the variables `relative_path_to_dir`, `file_url`, and `file_name` are derived from filesystem paths and inserted verbatim into HTML strings. An attacker who can create files or directories with names containing HTML/JavaScript metacharacters (e.g., `<script>alert(1)</script>`) on the server filesystem could trigger XSS when a user browses a directory listing. The `file_url` construction on line 687 also does not percent-encode the path, potentially introducing malformed URLs or further injection vectors.
findings.suggestion: Use `html.escape()` on all user-controlled or filesystem-derived values before inserting them into HTML output. For example: `file_name = html.escape(_file.name)` and `file_url = html.escape(self._prefix + '/' + rel_path)`. Also consider using a templating engine with auto-escaping.

findings.title: Potential path traversal when follow_symlinks is False via TOCTOU race
findings.description: In `_handle`, after calling `filepath.resolve()` on line 643, the code checks `filepath.relative_to(self._directory)` on line 645 to prevent path traversal. However, `resolve()` is called at check time, and `FileResponse` on line 668 subsequently opens the file independently. On some platforms or under specific race conditions (TOCTOU), a symlink could be swapped between the check and the open. Additionally, `filepath.resolve()` resolves symlinks by following them even when `self._follow_symlinks` is `False`—the check `filepath.relative_to(self._directory)` only verifies the resolved path is within the directory, but when follow_symlinks is False, a symlink pointing outside should be rejected. The actual rejection relies solely on the `relative_to` ValueError, which may not cover all edge cases if the resolved symlink destination is accidentally inside the allowed directory.
findings.suggestion: After resolving the path, also check that the path does not involve any symlink components when `follow_symlinks=False`. Consider using `os.path.realpath` combined with explicit symlink detection via `os.lstat` to detect and reject symlinks before serving. Pass the `follow_symlinks` parameter through to `FileResponse` if supported.

findings.title: `raise HTTPNotFound` missing parentheses raises class instead of instance
findings.description: On line 670, the code has `raise HTTPNotFound` without calling the constructor (missing parentheses). In Python, `raise SomeClass` will instantiate the class with no arguments, which may work for exceptions, but it is inconsistent with how HTTPNotFound is used elsewhere in the codebase (always with parentheses, e.g., line 648: `raise HTTPNotFound() from error`). While Python 3 does implicitly instantiate the class when raising, it bypasses any default argument initialization and may produce a different exception object than expected. This is a functional defect and style inconsistency that could produce unexpected behavior if HTTPNotFound's `__init__` has required logic that is triggered by normal instantiation.
findings.suggestion: Change `raise HTTPNotFound` to `raise HTTPNotFound()` to be consistent with other usages and ensure the exception is properly instantiated.

findings.title: ReDoS vulnerability via user-supplied regex in DynamicResource path patterns
findings.description: The `DynamicResource.__init__` method (lines 422-453) allows users to specify arbitrary regex patterns in route definitions via the `{var:regex}` syntax. On line 435, `match.group('re')` is extracted from the route path and inserted directly into the compiled regex pattern without any sanitization. A developer registering a route with a carefully crafted regex (e.g., `{x:(a+)+}`) could cause catastrophic backtracking when the regex is matched against incoming request paths, leading to denial of service. While this is controlled by developers rather than end users, it is still a risk in environments where route definitions are dynamic or semi-trusted.
findings.suggestion: Consider validating user-supplied regex patterns for known catastrophic backtracking patterns, or use a timeout mechanism for regex matching. At minimum, document this risk clearly.

findings.title: Path traversal bypass in `url_for` version hashing when follow_symlinks is False
findings.description: In `StaticResource.url_for` (lines 558-592), when `append_version=True`, the code resolves the filepath at line 577 and then checks `filepath.relative_to(self._directory)` on line 579 to prevent path traversal. However, this check happens on the resolved (symlink-followed) path, even when `self._follow_symlinks` is False. If `filepath.resolve()` follows a symlink to a location that happens to be a subdirectory of `self._directory` (e.g., a symlink from inside the static dir pointing to another subdirectory of it), the check would pass and the file's hash would be computed and exposed—even though the symlink should be rejected by the serve logic. This inconsistency between `url_for` and `_handle` means version hashes can be returned for files that cannot actually be served.
findings.suggestion: Apply the same symlink detection logic in `url_for` as in `_handle`, explicitly checking for symlink components when `follow_symlinks=False` before reading the file content.

findings.title: Shared mutable `HTTP_NOT_FOUND` instance as class-level singleton
findings.description: On line 979, `HTTP_NOT_FOUND = HTTPNotFound()` creates a single shared instance of `HTTPNotFound` at the class level. This instance is returned from `resolve()` on line 1027 via `MatchInfoError(self.HTTP_NOT_FOUND)`. If `HTTPNotFound` stores any mutable request-specific state, or if the `MatchInfoError`/`MatchInfoError` wrapper modifies the exception object, this could lead to state corruption across concurrent requests. While `HTTPNotFound` is typically stateless, this pattern is fragile and violates the principle of not sharing mutable state between requests.
findings.suggestion: Instantiate `HTTPNotFound()` fresh on each call within `resolve()` rather than reusing a shared class-level instance, to avoid any risk of state bleed between requests.

findings.title: Path traversal via os.path.normpath on absolute paths
findings.description: The `get_path` method uses `os.path.normpath(os.path.join(*scope['path'].split('/')))` to sanitize the incoming path. When the request path starts with '/', `scope['path'].split('/')` produces an empty string as the first element, so `os.path.join('', ...)` is used. However, if an attacker provides a path like '//absolute' or certain crafted paths, `os.path.normpath` can produce an absolute path (starting with '/') or a path beginning with the root directory separator. More critically, on Windows, `os.path.join` with an absolute path component discards previous components, allowing directory traversal. Additionally, `normpath` resolves '..' but `get_path` itself does not verify the result stays within any directory — that check is deferred to `lookup_path`. On POSIX, if `scope['path']` is '/etc/passwd', `split('/')` gives `['', 'etc', 'passwd']`, and `os.path.join('', 'etc', 'passwd')` gives `'etc/passwd'` which is fine, but on Windows or with UNC paths the behavior differs. The real risk is that `normpath` alone without a subsequent containment check in `get_path` relies entirely on `lookup_path`'s `commonprefix` check, which is bypassable (see next finding).
findings.suggestion: Strip leading slashes and validate that the normalized path does not start with '..' or '/'. Return a relative path and ensure it is always treated as relative when joined in lookup_path.

findings.title: Path traversal via os.path.commonprefix directory containment bypass
findings.description: `os.path.commonprefix` is a purely string-based operation and does not understand directory boundaries. For example, if `directory` is `/srv/static` and `full_path` is `/srv/static_evil/file.txt`, then `commonprefix(['/srv/static_evil/file.txt', '/srv/static'])` returns `/srv/static`, which equals `directory`, so the check passes and the file outside the intended directory would be served. This allows a path traversal attack where files in sibling directories whose names share a prefix with the intended static directory could be read.
findings.suggestion: Replace `os.path.commonprefix` with a proper directory containment check. Use `os.path.commonpath([full_path, directory]) == directory` (Python 3.5+), or verify that `full_path.startswith(directory + os.sep)` or `full_path == directory` after ensuring both are fully resolved absolute paths.

findings.title: Race condition in config_checked flag leads to duplicate check_config execution
findings.description: The `config_checked` flag is read and then set in a non-atomic fashion within an async context. If multiple concurrent requests arrive before `check_config` completes, all of them will observe `config_checked == False` and each will call `check_config()` concurrently. While this is mostly a performance issue (redundant checks), it could also mask errors if the directory state changes between checks, and it is not thread-safe if `config_checked` is accessed from multiple threads.
findings.suggestion: Use an asyncio.Lock or set the flag before awaiting `check_config()`, or use an asyncio.Event to signal completion to waiters.

findings.title: PermissionError incorrectly mapped to HTTP 401 instead of 403
findings.description: When a `PermissionError` occurs while looking up a path (e.g., the process lacks read permission on a file or directory), the code raises `HTTPException(status_code=401)`. HTTP 401 means 'Unauthorized' and implies that authentication could grant access. HTTP 403 'Forbidden' is the semantically correct response for permission errors at the OS level. Returning 401 could mislead clients into attempting authentication when none would help.
findings.suggestion: Change `raise HTTPException(status_code=401)` to `raise HTTPException(status_code=403)` to correctly indicate that the server understands the request but refuses to authorize it.

findings.title: follow_symlink=True disables symlink resolution allowing symlink escape
findings.description: When `follow_symlink=True`, the code uses `os.path.abspath(joined_path)` instead of `os.path.realpath(joined_path)`. `os.path.abspath` does not resolve symlinks; it only normalizes the path lexically. This means a symlink inside the static directory pointing outside it will not be detected by the subsequent `commonprefix` check, because the check compares the lexically-normalized path (which stays inside the directory) rather than the real path. This allows symlinks within the static directory to serve arbitrary files from outside the directory.
findings.suggestion: Even when `follow_symlink=True`, consider using `os.path.realpath` to resolve the actual path for the containment check, or at minimum document the security implications clearly. If symlink following is intentional, the containment check using `commonprefix` against the `abspath` version is still a string comparison and may be circumvented.

findings.title: RSA-PSS salt length uses digest_size attribute instead of digest_size instance value
findings.description: In RSAPSSAlgorithm.sign() and verify(), `self.hash_alg.digest_size` is accessed on the hash class itself (e.g., `hashes.SHA256`), not on an instance. The `hashes.SHA256` class from cryptography does not have a `digest_size` attribute as a class-level integer — this attribute exists on hashlib hash objects, not cryptography hash algorithm classes. This will raise an `AttributeError` at runtime when `sign()` or `verify()` is called, since `self.hash_alg` is stored as the class (e.g., `hashes.SHA256`), not an instance. The correct approach is to use `padding.PSS.MAX_LENGTH` or compute the digest size from the hash algorithm instance.
findings.suggestion: Use `padding.PSS.MAX_LENGTH` for the salt_length parameter (which is the RFC-recommended maximum), or instantiate the hash and access its digest_size: `self.hash_alg().digest_size`. For example: `salt_length=padding.PSS.MAX_LENGTH` or `salt_length=self.hash_alg().digest_size`.

findings.title: Incorrect string formatting in InvalidKeyError constructor for EC key 'd' parameter length check
findings.description: At line 505-507, the `InvalidKeyError` is raised with positional format arguments (`len(x)` and `curve`) that are never interpolated into the message string. The string `"D should be {} bytes for curve {}"` uses `str.format()`-style placeholders, but these are passed as extra positional arguments to the `InvalidKeyError` constructor, not to `.format()`. As a result, the error message will literally read `"D should be {} bytes for curve {}"` without substituting the actual values, providing no useful diagnostic information.
findings.suggestion: Use an f-string or explicit `.format()` call: `raise InvalidKeyError(f"D should be {len(x)} bytes for curve {curve}")`

findings.title: NoneAlgorithm.verify() always returns False instead of True for empty signatures
findings.description: The `NoneAlgorithm.verify()` method always returns `False`, even for a valid 'none' algorithm token with an empty signature. This means that if a caller uses `verify()` on a 'none' algorithm token that was legitimately signed with `NoneAlgorithm.sign()` (which returns `b""`), the verification will always fail. The correct behavior for the 'none' algorithm is to accept any token regardless of the signature (or specifically accept empty signatures), returning `True`. The consistent returning of `False` means callers may implement workarounds or bypass checks, potentially weakening the overall verification logic.
findings.suggestion: For the 'none' algorithm, `verify()` should return `True` (or optionally check that `sig == b""`) to be consistent with the signing behavior. However, care must be taken to ensure that the 'none' algorithm is explicitly disallowed in contexts where security is required.

findings.title: RSAAlgorithm.prepare_key() silently swallows exceptions other than ValueError when loading PEM keys
findings.description: In `RSAAlgorithm.prepare_key()`, when the key does not start with `b"ssh-rsa"`, `load_pem_private_key()` is called. If it raises a `ValueError` (indicating it's not a private key), `load_pem_public_key()` is tried. However, other exceptions (e.g., `TypeError`, `UnsupportedAlgorithm`) from `load_pem_private_key()` would propagate unhandled. Additionally, if `load_pem_public_key()` also fails, its exception propagates without a clear error message. A malformed key could produce confusing error messages without clear indication of what went wrong.
findings.suggestion: Catch broader exceptions and provide clear error messages, or explicitly validate the key format before attempting to load. Also handle `cryptography.exceptions.UnsupportedAlgorithm` appropriately.

findings.title: RSAAlgorithm.to_jwk() uses fragile heuristic to detect public key
findings.description: In `RSAAlgorithm.to_jwk()`, the check `getattr(key_obj, 'verify', None)` is used to detect a public RSA key. However, the `Algorithm` base class itself also defines a `verify` method, and many Python objects may have a `verify` attribute. The RSAPrivateKey class also has a `private_numbers` method, and the check for private keys uses `getattr(key_obj, 'private_numbers', None)`. Since Python functions are truthy, a private key that also has a `verify` attribute (which RSA private keys don't typically expose directly) might be misidentified. More robust would be to use `isinstance(key_obj, RSAPublicKey)` checks.
findings.suggestion: Replace the heuristic checks with explicit `isinstance(key_obj, RSAPrivateKey)` and `isinstance(key_obj, RSAPublicKey)` checks for clarity and correctness.

findings.title: SQL injection via unsanitized name_filter parameter in ilike query
findings.description: The `name_filter` parameter is taken directly from the query string and embedded into an `ilike` pattern via an f-string: `orm.User.name.ilike(f'%{name_filter}%')`. While SQLAlchemy's `ilike` method parameterizes the overall query value, the wildcard characters `%` and `_` within the user-supplied `name_filter` value act as SQL LIKE wildcards and are not escaped. An attacker can supply a crafted `name_filter` such as `_` or `%` to match arbitrary users or construct patterns that enumerate all users, bypassing the intent of name filtering. Depending on the database backend, this can also cause excessive query cost (denial of service via wildcard explosion). Additionally, if the ORM layer ever changes to raw SQL interpolation, this becomes a full SQL injection vector.
findings.suggestion: Escape SQL LIKE wildcard characters (`%`, `_`, `\`) in `name_filter` before embedding it in the ilike pattern, or use SQLAlchemy's `contains` / `like` with escaped patterns. For example: `name_filter_escaped = name_filter.replace('\\', '\\\\').replace('%', '\\%').replace('_', '\\_')` and then pass as `ilike(f'%{name_filter_escaped}%', escape='\\')`.

Specifically, `rendered_content` is initialized to `None` on line 291, and if `rendering_result is None` (which the code checks on line 292), `rendered_content` remains `None`. The function then returns `rendered_content` (line 297) which can be `None`. Any caller that uses the return value as a `str` without checking for `None` will experience a `TypeError` or `AttributeError` at runtime.
findings.suggestion: Fix the return type annotation to `Optional[str]` and ensure all callers handle the `None` case appropriately, or raise an exception when rendering fails instead of returning `None`.

findings.description: At line 1640, `assert isinstance(value, int)` is used to narrow the type of `value` after the preceding conditional checks. However, the logic at line 1638 is `if isinstance(value, str) or value <= 0`, which means: if value is a string AND not in special_values_map (from line 1636), OR value is not a string AND value <= 0, raise an error. After line 1638, the only remaining case is a non-string value > 0, which could be any numeric type such as float. The `assert` on line 1640 is a type assertion that Python will silently skip when run with the `-O` (optimize) flag, potentially allowing non-integer values (e.g., floats) to slip through and be returned as the `Optional[int]` return type, causing type contract violations downstream. Additionally, if `value` is a non-str, non-int numeric type (e.g., float) that is > 0, the assert would fire in debug mode, producing an AssertionError rather than a user-friendly `RequestVariableConversionError`.
findings.suggestion: Replace the `assert isinstance(value, int)` with an explicit check and raise `RequestVariableConversionError(setting_name, value)` if the value is not an integer, ensuring the guard works in all Python execution modes.

findings.description: The second subquery in the UNION ALL (lines 1545-1557) queries `zerver_message` where `m.recipient_id=%(my_recipient_id)s` but does NOT filter by `um.user_profile_id` or any equivalent user-scoping on the message table. This means for 1:1 PMs where the current user is the recipient, it fetches ALL messages sent to that recipient ID, regardless of whether the current user is actually the intended recipient. In a Zulip deployment where recipient IDs are shared (e.g., group recipients), this could surface message IDs from conversations the user should not see. The SQL itself is parameterized correctly against injection, but the logic exposes more data than intended for the second subquery.

findings.title: Off-by-one in message_visibility_limit index calculation
findings.description: At line 1457, the code uses `[realm.message_visibility_limit - 1]` as an index into an ordered queryset to find the first visible message. The intent is to find the Nth most recent message (where N = message_visibility_limit), making everything before it invisible. Using `[realm.message_visibility_limit - 1]` as the 0-based index in a descending order queryset means it retrieves the message at position N-1 (0-indexed), i.e., the Nth most recent message. If the intent is that users can see the most recent `message_visibility_limit` messages, then the first visible message should be at index `message_visibility_limit - 1` (the Nth most recent), which appears correct. However, if `realm.message_visibility_limit` is 0, this would result in index `-1`, fetching the last (oldest) message rather than raising an error, potentially making all messages visible instead of none. The `maybe_update_first_visible_message_id` function checks `recent_messages_count > 0` but not `message_visibility_limit > 0`.
findings.suggestion: Add a guard to ensure `realm.message_visibility_limit > 0` before using it as an index, or handle the edge case where it could be 0 or negative.

findings.title: Mutable default argument for `config` in `File.__init__`
findings.description: The `File.__init__` method uses a mutable dictionary `{}` as the default value for the `config` parameter. In Python, default argument values are evaluated once at function definition time, not on each call. If any caller mutates the `config` dictionary (e.g., by calling `config.update(...)` or assigning keys), all subsequent calls that rely on the default will share and observe those mutations. This can lead to unpredictable behavior across multiple `File` instances that use the default config.
findings.suggestion: Replace `config={}` with `config=None` and set `self._config = config if config is not None else {}` inside the method body.

Although line 112-113 strips Windows-style absolute paths (UNC and drive-letter paths), it does not strip relative path traversal components such as `../` or encoded equivalents. A malicious actor could supply a filename like `../../etc/cron.d/backdoor` and, when the server has `UPLOAD_KEEP_FILENAME=True`, write a file to an arbitrary location on the filesystem outside of `UPLOAD_DIR`.
findings.suggestion: After computing `fname`, apply `os.path.basename(fname)` to strip any directory components, and then validate that `os.path.realpath(path)` starts with `os.path.realpath(file_dir)` before opening the file.

findings.title: StringAgg delimiter inserted unescaped into SQL template via string formatting
findings.description: The `StringAgg` class uses a template string `"%(function)s(%(distinct)s%(expressions)s, '%(delimiter)s'%(ordering)s)"` where the `delimiter` parameter is interpolated directly into the SQL string without any escaping or parameterization. If a caller passes a delimiter containing a single quote or other SQL metacharacters (e.g., `"'"`, `"'; DROP TABLE--"`), the resulting SQL will be malformed or exploitable. Because Django's template substitution for aggregate `extra` kwargs uses Python string `%` formatting rather than database-level parameterization, the delimiter value is embedded verbatim into the SQL query string. An attacker who can influence the `delimiter` argument (e.g., via user-controlled input passed to `StringAgg`) can break out of the string literal and inject arbitrary SQL.
findings.suggestion: Do not embed the delimiter directly into the SQL template string. Instead, pass the delimiter as a bound parameter using the database's parameterization mechanism, or at minimum enforce strict validation (e.g., ensure the delimiter is a single safe character and escape any SQL special characters). Consider overriding `as_sql` to emit the delimiter as a proper query parameter.

findings.title: convert_value returns [] for falsy non-None values such as empty list, potentially masking a valid NULL vs empty distinction
findings.description: Both `ArrayAgg.convert_value` and `JSONBAgg.convert_value` use `if not value:` to guard their return. This condition is true for `None` (NULL from the database, i.e., no rows matched), but also for any other falsy value such as an empty list `[]`. If the database ever returns an actual empty list (which PostgreSQL ARRAY_AGG / JSONB_AGG can return as `'{}'` / `'[]'`), this branch would still return `[]`, which happens to be correct. However, the condition also catches `0`, `False`, and empty strings — none of which should occur as the aggregate result, but the logic is fragile. More critically, `StringAgg.convert_value` (line 60–63) returns `''` for any falsy value; if the aggregate legitimately returns an empty string (possible when aggregating empty-string fields), the NULL case and the empty-result case are indistinguishable.
findings.suggestion: Use an explicit `if value is None:` check instead of `if not value:` to correctly distinguish a SQL NULL result from a legitimate falsy aggregate result (such as an empty string or zero).
